stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 at 39+2 weeks is admitted to your regional birth suite for artificial rupture of membranes to augment prolonged latent labour. Immediately after rupture, a loop of pulsating cord is felt below the presenting part at the introitus. Her previous births were normal vaginal deliveries at term. The foetus is estimated at 3.4 kg on scan last week.

On examination the vertex is at station -2 and the cervix is 5 cm dilated with a soft tucked-in loop of cord clearly palpable in front of the head. The mother is anxious but comfortable. Continuous cardiotocography shows a foetal heart rate baseline of 90/min with deep prolonged decelerations. The on-call obstetric registrar is 4 minutes away and the anaesthetist is at the head of the bed. The theatre team is being activated with a Category 1 caesarean call.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 108/min, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C; foetal heart rate 90/min with prolonged decelerations
data_table.Examination: Cord palpable below the presenting part at the introitus, cervix 5 cm dilated, vertex station -2
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocography as above; pre-existing group and hold in place

lead_in: While waiting for theatre, what is the single most appropriate immediate manoeuvre?

options.text: Ask the mother to bear down with the next contraction to complete a rapid spontaneous vaginal birth in the birth room without transfer to theatre
options.rationale: Instrumental or spontaneous vaginal delivery is only appropriate when the cervix is fully dilated and the head is low; at 5 cm dilatation vaginal birth is not achievable. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Give a single intravenous dose of ergometrine 250 micrograms to expel the foetus rapidly through the cervix as a temporising measure
options.rationale: Ergometrine causes uterine hyperstimulation and is contraindicated with a live foetus in utero; it would worsen foetal compromise. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Cut and clamp the prolapsed cord at the introitus to prevent further cord exposure and vasospasm during the transfer to theatre
options.rationale: Cutting the cord terminates foetal circulation and is only ever considered after delivery; it must never be done with a live foetus in utero. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Elevate the presenting part with the examining hand, place the mother in knee-chest position and fill the bladder with 500 mL warm saline via catheter
options.rationale: Elevating the presenting part off the cord, gravity positioning and bladder filling all reduce cord compression while theatre is prepared for Category 1 caesarean. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical Cord Prolapse)

options.text: Start intravenous oxytocin infusion at 12 milliunits per minute to accelerate labour and shorten time to delivery
options.rationale: Oxytocin augmentation increases contractions and cord compression; tocolysis (e.g. terbutaline) is the correct pharmacological adjunct while awaiting theatre. (Source: RANZCOG Umbilical Cord Prolapse)

explanation.summary: Umbilical cord prolapse after artificial rupture of membranes requires immediate action to relieve compression while a Category 1 caesarean is arranged. The examining hand elevates the presenting part off the cord and remains in situ until delivery. The mother is placed in knee-chest or steep left lateral Trendelenburg, and bladder filling with 500 to 700 mL of warm saline via an indwelling catheter reduces cord pressure. Tocolysis with subcutaneous terbutaline 250 micrograms can be used if there is contraction-related deceleration and delivery is delayed. Cord handling should be minimised to avoid vasospasm; if the cord is outside the introitus, replace it gently in the vagina. Delivery within 30 minutes of diagnosis is targeted.
key_points: Elevate the presenting part with the examining hand and keep it there.
Knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg reduces gravitational cord pressure.
Bladder filling with warm saline further offloads the cord.
Tocolysis with terbutaline is the adjunct if delivery is delayed.
explanation.pearls: After ARM-triggered cord prolapse, keep the examining hand elevating the presenting part, position knee-chest and fill the bladder with warm saline while theatre is prepared for Category 1 caesarean.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Obstetric emergencies - Cord prolapse

subtopic_detail: GBS intrapartum prophylaxis with penicillin allergy
stem:
A 29-year-old G2P1 at 39+0 weeks is admitted to your metropolitan birth suite in early spontaneous labour. Her routine antenatal vagino-rectal swab at 36 weeks was positive for group B streptococcus. She has a documented history of anaphylaxis to penicillin at age 12, treated with intramuscular adrenaline, and has never been formally allergy tested since. She has no known allergy to clindamycin or vancomycin. Her previous birth in New Zealand was uncomplicated with intrapartum benzylpenicillin, which she cannot recall clearly.

On examination she is comfortable, cervix is 4 cm dilated and effaced, membranes intact, vertex presentation at station 0. Contractions are every 4 minutes lasting 40 seconds. Cardiotocography is reassuring. Her medical notes flag the anaphylaxis with a red bracelet. Local antimicrobial stewardship policy requires you to give intrapartum prophylaxis to this patient.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 92/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C; foetal heart rate 138/min baseline, reassuring
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, effaced, membranes intact, vertex at station 0
data_table.Investigations: 36-week vagino-rectal swab positive for group B streptococcus; sensitivity report not available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic choice?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery with adrenaline available at the bedside
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin is contraindicated after documented anaphylaxis to penicillin; adrenaline preparation does not make deliberate re-exposure appropriate. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus prophylaxis)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus prophylaxis

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every 8 hours until delivery because cephalosporin cross-reactivity is under 2 percent
options.rationale: Cephalosporins are avoided after documented penicillin anaphylaxis; a non-beta-lactam is preferred when the isolate's clindamycin sensitivity is unknown. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus prophylaxis)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus prophylaxis

options.text: Oral azithromycin 500 mg once at admission as an equivalent alternative to intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis
options.rationale: Oral macrolides do not reliably reach adequate foetal and amniotic fluid levels for GBS prophylaxis; the AU standard is intravenous therapy. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus prophylaxis)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus prophylaxis

options.text: No antibiotic prophylaxis, and observe the neonate for 48 hours with early paediatric review given the maternal allergy history
options.rationale: Screen-positive women require intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis; withholding it increases early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus prophylaxis)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus prophylaxis

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 20 mg per kilogram (maximum 2 g) infused over 2 hours, repeated every 8 hours until delivery
options.rationale: With documented penicillin anaphylaxis and unknown clindamycin susceptibility, AU guidelines recommend IV vancomycin 20 mg/kg (max 2 g) 8-hourly until delivery for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis. (Source: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus prophylaxis)
source_refs: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus prophylaxis

explanation.summary: Universal antenatal culture-based screening for group B streptococcus is the AU standard between 35 and 37 weeks. Screen-positive women receive intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis, ideally starting at least 4 hours before delivery. First-line is intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g 4-hourly. In non-severe penicillin allergy (rash without anaphylaxis) IV cefazolin is used. In documented anaphylaxis, treatment depends on isolate sensitivity: IV clindamycin if the isolate is confirmed clindamycin-sensitive, otherwise IV vancomycin 20 mg/kg (max 2 g) 8-hourly. Empirical clindamycin is discouraged because resistance rates approach 20 percent. Neonatal observation is guided by mother's antibiotic duration and neonatal risk factors, not a substitute for prophylaxis.
key_points: First-line intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is IV benzylpenicillin 3 g then 1.8 g 4-hourly.
Cefazolin for non-severe penicillin allergy; vancomycin for anaphylaxis without known clindamycin sensitivity.
Empirical clindamycin is discouraged due to ~20 percent resistance.
Effective prophylaxis requires at least 4 hours before delivery.
explanation.pearls: In labouring GBS-positive women with prior penicillin anaphylaxis and unknown clindamycin susceptibility, give IV vancomycin 20 mg/kg (max 2 g) every 8 hours until delivery.

sources.label: Australian eTG: Antibiotic - Group B streptococcus prophylaxis
RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus in Pregnancy

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P1 has just delivered a live female infant of 3.6 kg at 40+3 weeks by unassisted vaginal birth in your regional birth suite. Her pregnancy was uncomplicated except for gestational hypertension controlled on labetalol 200 mg twice daily, with blood pressures around 130/85 mmHg over the last month. Her first delivery 3 years ago was complicated by a primary postpartum haemorrhage of 1.5 litres treated with a bimanual uterine compression and further uterotonics.

Cord clamping was delayed by 90 seconds and the baby is doing skin-to-skin on her chest. The placenta has not yet delivered. She has an intravenous cannula in place and observations are stable. She has no known drug allergy and is not asthmatic. The midwife is preparing to administer the routine third-stage uterotonic and asks you which agent to draw up.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 132/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus at umbilicus, small trickle of blood at the introitus, no active haemorrhage

lead_in: What is the most appropriate uterotonic to administer now?

options.text: Intramuscular oxytocin 10 units into the anterolateral thigh as prophylactic active management of the third stage
options.rationale: AU active management of the third stage uses IM oxytocin 10 units with delivery of the anterior shoulder or after the birth, avoiding ergometrine in hypertensive women. (Source: RANZCOG Prevention Detection and Management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG Prevention Detection and Management of PPH

options.text: Intramuscular Syntometrine (ergometrine 500 micrograms plus oxytocin 5 units) as combined prophylactic active management
options.rationale: Syntometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy because the ergometrine component can precipitate severe hypertension. (Source: RANZCOG Prevention Detection and Management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG Prevention Detection and Management of PPH

options.text: Rectal misoprostol 800 micrograms as an equivalent to intramuscular oxytocin for prophylactic third-stage management
options.rationale: Misoprostol is second-line where oxytocin is unavailable; it has more side effects and less consistent uterine tone than parenteral oxytocin. (Source: RANZCOG Prevention Detection and Management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG Prevention Detection and Management of PPH

options.text: Intravenous carboprost 250 micrograms slow push as prophylactic uterotonic in women at risk of postpartum haemorrhage
options.rationale: Carboprost is a treatment for ongoing postpartum haemorrhage in AU practice, not a prophylactic agent; it is IM-only and contraindicated in severe asthma. (Source: RANZCOG Prevention Detection and Management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG Prevention Detection and Management of PPH

options.text: Withhold routine uterotonic and use physiological management given the delayed cord clamping already performed
options.rationale: Delayed cord clamping is compatible with active management; skipping the uterotonic increases haemorrhage risk, particularly in women with previous PPH. (Source: RANZCOG Prevention Detection and Management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG Prevention Detection and Management of PPH

explanation.summary: Active management of the third stage of labour combines a prophylactic uterotonic, controlled cord traction and uterine massage. In Australia, IM oxytocin 10 units is the standard uterotonic and is given with delivery of the anterior shoulder or immediately after birth. Syntometrine (ergometrine 500 micrograms plus oxytocin 5 units) offers slightly lower blood loss but is contraindicated in hypertensive disorders because ergometrine can precipitate stroke. Misoprostol 600 to 800 micrograms is reserved for settings without cold-chain access to oxytocin. Delayed cord clamping of 1 to 3 minutes is compatible with active management and is standard practice. Women with prior PPH remain candidates for standard active management with a lower threshold for early uterotonic escalation.
key_points: IM oxytocin 10 units is the standard AU prophylactic uterotonic.
Syntometrine is contraindicated in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
Misoprostol is second-line where oxytocin is unavailable.
Delayed cord clamping is compatible with active management.
explanation.pearls: In a labouring woman with gestational hypertension, use IM oxytocin 10 units for third-stage prophylaxis rather than Syntometrine, which contains ergometrine and is contraindicated.

sources.label: RANZCOG Prevention Detection and Management of PPH

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic surgical choice after contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
A 33-year-old G3P1 is admitted to your metropolitan gynaecology unit at 7+2 weeks by dates with lower abdominal pain and light vaginal spotting for 12 hours. She had a right salpingectomy 4 years ago for a ruptured tubal ectopic that presented with haemorrhagic shock. She conceived spontaneously this cycle and is desperate to preserve future fertility. She has no history of pelvic inflammatory disease and no ongoing medications.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable but pale, with left iliac fossa tenderness and cervical excitation. Serum beta-hCG is 6800 IU/L and rising 60 percent from a level 48 hours ago. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a 3.0 cm adnexal mass adjacent to the ipsilateral (left) ovary with foetal cardiac activity and a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her partner is present and understands the situation. She has requested surgical management as she cannot commit to weekly follow-up.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, left iliac fossa tenderness, cervical excitation, no rebound
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta-hCG 6800 IU/L; TVUSS: empty uterus, 3.0 cm left adnexal mass with foetal cardiac activity, small pouch of Douglas fluid; blood group A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management?

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy on the left tube to preserve tubal function and future spontaneous fertility with weekly beta-hCG follow-up
options.rationale: With prior contralateral salpingectomy this is her only remaining tube; salpingostomy carries a 5 to 15 percent risk of persistent trophoblast plus higher recurrence in the same tube, both worse than salpingectomy plus IVF for future fertility. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy on the left tube with counselling about need for in vitro fertilisation for future conception
options.rationale: After a prior contralateral salpingectomy the affected side is the only remaining tube; salpingectomy avoids persistent trophoblast and recurrence risk, and IVF is the fertility plan given loss of tubes. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre with weekly beta-hCG follow-up until non-pregnant range
options.rationale: Methotrexate is contraindicated when there is foetal cardiac activity or beta-hCG above 5000 IU/L per RANZCOG criteria; both apply here. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Expectant management with 48-hourly beta-hCG monitoring while she considers her options over the coming week
options.rationale: Expectant management requires beta-hCG below 1500 IU/L and downtrending; this patient's beta-hCG is 6800 IU/L and rising. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Laparotomy with total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for definitive management
options.rationale: Radical surgery is not appropriate for a haemodynamically stable ectopic; laparoscopy is minimally invasive and preserves the uterus and ovaries for potential IVF. (Source: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Surgical management of tubal ectopic pregnancy in Australia is laparoscopy first-line. The choice between salpingectomy (removing the affected tube) and salpingostomy (opening the tube and evacuating the ectopic) is guided by contralateral tube status and future fertility plans. When the contralateral tube is normal, salpingectomy is preferred because salpingostomy leaves 5 to 15 percent persistent trophoblast requiring further intervention and does not improve future spontaneous conception rates. When the contralateral tube has already been removed (prior salpingectomy), the affected tube is the last remaining tube - salpingectomy is still preferred because recurrence risk in a compromised tube is high, and IVF becomes the fertility plan. Methotrexate is contraindicated when there is foetal cardiac activity, beta-hCG above 5000 IU/L, mass over 3.5 cm, significant pain or haemorrhage.
key_points: Laparoscopy is first-line surgical management for tubal ectopic.
Salpingectomy preferred over salpingostomy when tube function is impaired or contralateral tube absent.
Methotrexate contraindicated with cardiac activity or beta-hCG above 5000 IU/L.
IVF is the fertility plan after bilateral salpingectomy.
explanation.pearls: In tubal ectopic with prior contralateral salpingectomy, salpingectomy of the last remaining tube plus IVF outperforms salpingostomy for cumulative reproductive success.

sources.label: RANZCOG Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

stem:
A 36-year-old G2P2 is reviewed on the postnatal ward day 3 after an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39+5 weeks. Her antenatal course was unremarkable, blood pressures always below 130/80 mmHg and no proteinuria. Today she reports right upper quadrant pain, nausea and one episode of vomiting for the last 12 hours. She has been well hydrated and has been mobilising.

On examination she is diaphoretic. Right upper quadrant is tender without peritonism, uterus is well contracted and lochia is normal. Reflexes are 3+ with two beats of clonus at the right ankle. There is no rash. Her recent bloods show haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-160), platelets 62 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 480 U/L (5-30), AST 520 U/L (10-40), LDH 780 U/L (110-250), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90), fibrinogen 3.4 g/L (1.5-4.0), INR 1.1 (0.9-1.2) and urine dipstick 3+ protein. A blood film shows fragmented red cells.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure 178/112 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, right upper quadrant tender without peritonism, hyperreflexia with clonus, uterus contracted, normal lochia
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L (115-160); platelets 62 x10^9/L (150-400); ALT 480 U/L (5-30); AST 520 U/L (10-40); LDH 780 U/L (110-250); creatinine 118 mcmol/L (45-90); fibrinogen 3.4 g/L (1.5-4.0); urine 3+ protein; blood film fragments

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g plus metronidazole 500 mg empirically for suspected postnatal endometritis and cholangitis
options.rationale: Sepsis is a differential but the haematology, liver enzymes, hypertension, hyperreflexia and proteinuria are classic for postpartum HELLP; empirical antibiotics alone will not address the underlying pathology. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms and firm uterine fundal massage for suspected occult postpartum haemorrhage
options.rationale: Uterus is contracted with normal lochia; there is no active haemorrhage and ergometrine is contraindicated with severe hypertension. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g per hour infusion plus intravenous labetalol 20 mg for blood pressure control
options.rationale: Postpartum HELLP with severe range hypertension and hyperreflexia needs magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis and rapid antihypertensive control; both are SOMANZ first-line. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Urgent abdominal ultrasound looking for gallstones and biliary dilatation before starting any specific therapy for her presentation
options.rationale: Delaying treatment for imaging in a woman with severe postpartum hypertension and hyperreflexia risks eclampsia and stroke; treat first, image second. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days to accelerate platelet recovery in postpartum HELLP
options.rationale: Steroid therapy for HELLP has not been shown to improve maternal outcomes and is not part of the SOMANZ pathway; magnesium and blood pressure control are the immediate priorities. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)

explanation.summary: HELLP (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) can present or worsen postpartum in up to 30 percent of cases. Diagnostic criteria include microangiopathic haemolysis (fragments on film, LDH above 600 U/L, low haptoglobin), AST or ALT above twice normal, and platelets below 100 x10^9/L. Presentation may lack antenatal hypertension. Treatment is the same as for antenatal severe pre-eclampsia: magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g per hour for seizure prophylaxis, rapid antihypertensive control (labetalol IV 20 mg boluses, hydralazine, or oral nifedipine per SOMANZ), fluid restriction to avoid pulmonary oedema, and close monitoring for hepatic haematoma or DIC. Steroids and platelet transfusion are not routine unless bleeding or platelets below 20 x10^9/L for delivery.
key_points: Postpartum HELLP can present without antenatal hypertension.
Diagnostic triad: haemolysis, transaminase elevation, thrombocytopenia.
Treat with magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/hour plus rapid antihypertensive.
Steroids not routine; platelet transfusion only for active bleeding or under 20.
explanation.pearls: Postpartum HELLP without antecedent hypertension needs magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g/hour plus IV labetalol; steroids and imaging come later.

stem:
A 30-year-old G3P2 at 32+4 weeks presents to your regional birth suite with sudden severe constant lower abdominal pain and 400 mL of dark vaginal bleeding for 30 minutes. She smokes 15 cigarettes daily. Her antenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks reported a fundal placenta. She has hypertension in this pregnancy managed on labetalol 200 mg twice daily.

On examination she is pale and clammy, uterus is woody hard and tender between contractions, with tender points more marked over the left uterine wall. Foetal parts are difficult to palpate. Cardiotocography shows late decelerations with reduced variability and a foetal heart rate baseline of 110/min. Speculum reveals dark blood at the introitus, cervix appears closed. Point-of-care coagulation shows fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2.0-4.5), platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400) and INR 1.4 (0.9-1.2). A pre-existing group and hold is on file. Two large-bore intravenous lines have been sited.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97 percent on 6 L/min via face mask, temperature 36.7 degrees C; foetal heart rate 110/min with late decelerations
data_table.Examination: Pale and clammy, woody hard tender uterus, foetal parts difficult to palpate, closed cervix on speculum, dark vaginal blood
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L (115-160); fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2.0-4.5); platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400); INR 1.4 (0.9-1.2); group A positive; crossmatch requested

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Transabdominal ultrasound in the birth suite to confirm placental location before any further intervention today
options.rationale: The clinical picture is diagnostic for concealed abruption with disseminated intravascular coagulation and foetal compromise; delaying delivery for ultrasound is unsafe. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Nifedipine 20 mg orally to tocolyse for 48 hours plus intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg for foetal lung maturation
options.rationale: Tocolysis is contraindicated in abruption with coagulopathy and foetal compromise; delivery must proceed and antenatal steroids are given but do not delay delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Await further foetal cardiotocography over the next hour to confirm sustained pathological trace before mobilising theatre
options.rationale: Late decelerations with reduced variability plus concealed abruption already indicate significant foetal compromise; delay increases perinatal mortality. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol, correct coagulopathy with fibrinogen concentrate, and proceed to Category 1 caesarean delivery
options.rationale: Concealed abruption with hypovolaemia, DIC and foetal compromise mandates activation of MTP, coagulopathy correction and immediate operative delivery. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes as neuroprotection while awaiting further imaging results
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is only given if delivery can be delayed by at least 4 hours; here delivery must be immediate. (Source: RANZCOG Antepartum Haemorrhage)

explanation.summary: Placental abruption is a clinical diagnosis in a woman with painful bleeding, a tender woody uterus, foetal compromise on cardiotocography and features of coagulopathy. Bleeding may be revealed or concealed, and haemodynamic status can be worse than the visible loss suggests. Ultrasound has poor sensitivity and should not delay treatment. In contrast, placenta praevia typically presents with painless bleeding and a soft non-tender uterus. When abruption is complicated by coagulopathy and foetal compromise, immediate delivery (usually Category 1 caesarean unless the foetus is already dead and the mother is stable) is required, with activation of the massive transfusion protocol, correction of fibrinogen to at least 2.0 g/L using fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate, and early involvement of anaesthesia and haematology.
key_points: Painful bleeding with tender woody uterus and coagulopathy is abruption.
Ultrasound has poor sensitivity for abruption; do not delay delivery.
Correct fibrinogen to at least 2.0 g/L with concentrate or cryoprecipitate.
Category 1 caesarean when foetal compromise and coagulopathy coexist.
explanation.pearls: In painful antepartum bleeding with a woody uterus, foetal late decelerations and fibrinogen below 2 g/L, activate the massive transfusion protocol and proceed to Category 1 caesarean without waiting for ultrasound.

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism vs pulmonary embolism
stem:
A 34-year-old G3P2 at 39+6 weeks is in the second stage of labour after augmentation with intravenous oxytocin. As the head crowns she suddenly complains of feeling short of breath, becomes profoundly cyanotic and loses consciousness within 60 seconds. She had no known respiratory or cardiac history, no prior thromboembolism and no obesity. Prophylactic enoxaparin was ceased in early labour per protocol.

CPR is commenced immediately and a Code Blue is called. Bag-mask ventilation is difficult due to central cyanosis and pink frothy secretions from the mouth. Rhythm strip shows pulseless electrical activity. There is heavy vaginal blood loss estimated at 1200 mL in the last few minutes with no obvious source on inspection. Point-of-care coagulation shows fibrinogen 1.0 g/L (2.0-4.5), INR 2.4 (0.9-1.2) and platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400). Bedside transthoracic echocardiography by the anaesthetic registrar shows a dilated dyskinetic right ventricle with septal bowing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulseless electrical activity, no measurable blood pressure, SpO2 unrecordable on 15 L/min via bag-mask, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cyanotic, unresponsive, pink frothy oral secretions, heavy vaginal blood loss, dilated tender uterus
data_table.Investigations: Fibrinogen 1.0 g/L (2.0-4.5); INR 2.4 (0.9-1.2); platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400); TTE dilated dyskinetic right ventricle with septal bowing

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step alongside ongoing advanced life support?

options.text: Systemic thrombolysis with intravenous alteplase 100 mg infused over 90 minutes for suspected massive pulmonary embolism as the primary cause
options.rationale: The picture of sudden collapse during crowning with rapid coagulopathy and DIC is amniotic fluid embolism; thrombolysis would worsen the obstetric haemorrhage and is not indicated. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 5 mg bolus every 3 to 5 minutes to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure during the ongoing cardiac arrest
options.rationale: ANZCOR adrenaline dose in adult arrest is 1 mg (not 5 mg) every 3 to 5 minutes; 5 mg is not evidence-based and risks tachyarrhythmia. (Source: ANZCOR ALS Adult)

options.text: Insert a right internal jugular central venous oximetry catheter before any operative decision so that resuscitation therapy can be titrated
options.rationale: Line insertion is important but does not take priority over perimortem caesarean and coagulopathy correction, and adds no immediate treatment in this crisis. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

options.text: Continue closed-chest CPR alone and defer perimortem caesarean until return of spontaneous maternal circulation is confirmed on the rhythm strip
options.rationale: ANZCOR mandates perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes of arrest in a viable pregnancy; deferring until ROSC forgoes the aortocaval decompression that facilitates return. (Source: ANZCOR ALS Adult)

options.text: Perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes, activate massive transfusion with fibrinogen concentrate, and give inhaled pulmonary vasodilator for right ventricular support
options.rationale: AFE with cardiovascular collapse and DIC needs perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes, coagulopathy correction with fibrinogen concentrate, and pulmonary vasodilator plus inotrope support for the dyskinetic right ventricle. (Source: RANZCOG Amniotic Fluid Embolism)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) presents with sudden peripartum cardiovascular collapse, hypoxaemia and disseminated intravascular coagulation, often during or immediately after delivery. It is a clinical diagnosis; there is no confirmatory test acutely. Echocardiographic findings of a dilated dyskinetic right ventricle with septal bowing help distinguish AFE from primary obstetric haemorrhage (in which the right ventricle looks empty). Management is high-quality CPR per ANZCOR, perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes if there is no return of maternal circulation, activation of the massive transfusion protocol, correction of fibrinogen to at least 2 g/L (fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate), inhaled pulmonary vasodilator (e.g. nitric oxide) and inotrope support for right ventricular failure, and consideration of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in tertiary centres. Recovery is possible but maternal and neonatal mortality remain high.
key_points: AFE is a clinical diagnosis; treat empirically on the picture.
Perimortem caesarean within 4 minutes if no ROSC.
Correct fibrinogen to at least 2 g/L with concentrate or cryoprecipitate.
RV failure: inhaled pulmonary vasodilator plus inotrope; consider ECMO.
explanation.pearls: In peripartum arrest with pink frothy secretions, DIC and dyskinetic right ventricle on point-of-care echocardiography, treat as amniotic fluid embolism with perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes, MTP with fibrinogen concentrate, and pulmonary vasodilator support.
